Using the sequencer instructions, the PLC can direct the output devices to perform a cyclic chain of events. This is useful in an automated manufacturing environment where repetitive tasking is the bulk of the operations...

LESSON MENU
SEQUENCER INSTRUCTIONS
In this lesson, we will examine the sequencer instructions used by a PLC. First, let's discuss what a sequence is.
DISCUSSION
A sequence is an ordered list of items. In this case, a sequence is a data file with words in it. Contained in the words is a pattern of events being directed to a particular output.
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts

For example, let's say you want to turn on one laser for one second, turn on a second laser for two seconds, and then wait three seconds until repeating the process. The smallest stipulated time interval is one second, so each sequence should last for one second...
To do this, timers are normally used to increment a sequence every second. After the timer is set up, we need to generate our sequence.
Laser one is attached to output 0, bit 1 and laser two is attached to output 0, bit 3. These are the only bits that we will be using in the sequence. All other bits should remain zero.

Now we need to determine the length of the sequence. Count up the total time and divide by the timer length. In our example, one second (for laser one) plus two seconds (for laser two) plus three seconds (for the delay) equals six seconds. Six seconds divided by one second equals a sequence length of six...
The first sequence data item contains only one high bit. This turns laser one on for one second. Remember, each sequence data item is to the output port once a second, based on our timer.
The second and third data items have bit three set high, and all other bits off. This ensures that laser one is turned off and laser two is turned on for two seconds.
The last three sequence data items have all bits set to zero. Because of this, both lasers will be off for three seconds.

After you have reached the end of the sequence, the next output from the instruction will start back at the beginning of the sequence file. This cycle will continue until the sequence instruction settings are changed...
It is important to note that a timer does not need to be used. These instructions can be initiated by a series of met conditions.
The three instructions listed below are the sequencer instructions that we will examine. Each of these instructions provide important features to sequencing a PLC.
SQL - Sequencer Loadamming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts

This is the Sequencer Output (SQO) instruction, the most important of the three sequencer instructions. Sequencer Output requires six parameters: file, mask, destination, control, length, and position...
The file is the location of the sequencer data which will be sent to some specified destination. The Sequencer Output instruction uses 16-bits (1 word) at a time as a sequencer data item..
The next parameter is the mask. This indicates which bits you want sent to the destination. The value can be an actual value or a data element in memory.
The destination (dest) is a word location where the sequenced data will be sent. In most cases, this will be an output data file.

The control parameter indicates a data element in memory used to control the operation of the sequencer outputs. The data element contains three words. The first word contains status bits about the sequencing...
The second word indicates the length and current position of the sequencer file. Since these values can be modified, make sure you don't go outside a file range, to prevent errors from occurring...

The sequence status bits indicate different states of the sequencer instruction operation. The EN (enable bit) indicates that a low to high transition in the preceding logic path occurred which enabled the instruction to sequence once...

The DN (done bit) indicates that a sequence has occurred and is finished. The ER (error bit) indicates when there are errors in the parameter values to the instruction. This could be, for example, a negative length or position...
The last status bit, FD (found bit), is not used with this instruction. It is used with the next instruction we will examine, SQC.

The length and position parameters are stored in the control data element. Again, the length is the number of words in the file you are sequencing. The position indicates the address location in the sequence data file. The maximum length is 255...

Remember, when a low to high transition occurs preceding this instruction, the enable bit is set. The position is incremented, the next word in the sequence data file is read and sent to the destination, the enable bit is set low, and the done bit is set high...
What is the maximum length that you can specify to the Sequencer Output (SQO) instruction?
Remember, the maximum length is 255 words..................
TRY AGAIN!
The next instruction that we are going to look at is the Sequencer Compare (SQC) instruction. This instruction is used to compare a current value with a value stored in memory or an input value...

Many devices provide data about the current status of the device. This is sometimes referred to as diagnostics. If you know all the different diagnostic words that a device can send you, you can put them all in a data file...

When the PLC reads the inputs, a Sequencer Compare instruction can be used to compare the input data to each of the items in the sequence data file one by one. The position value can then be used to determine what the next action is...

When a match is made between the input data and a word in the sequence data file, the found bit (FD) is set in the control data file. Notice that all the parameters are the same except destination has been replaced by source...
The source indicates the data element location that will be used in the comparison with the sequence data file elements. Normally, this is an input data file element but it does not have to be...

All other parameters work the same as for the SQO instruction. When this instruction is called (when the preceding logic goes from low to high), the position is incremented. The value from the source is sent through the mask and compared to the data element in the current position of the sequencer data file...
If they match, the found bit is set high, and the instruction is finished. The instruction will be used again until another low to high logic transition occurs.
Which bit is set high when the source data word, through the mask, is equal to the currently pointed at data word in the sequencer file?
Remember, it is the found bit (FD) that is set high when the source data value matches the current value pointed to in the sequencer data file.
TRY AGAIN!
The last instruction that we will examine is the Sequencer Load instruction (SQL). This instruction is used to load data into a sequencer file.

The file parameter contains the sequencer data file to be modified. The source can be a file address, an I/O, a storage word address, or a program constant. The control, length, and position parameters work the same as for the SQO instruction...

When a low to high transition occurs before this instruction, the value at, or pointed to by, the source is moved into the current position of the sequencer data file and the position value is incremented...
Once the position value reaches the length, the position returns to zero. The instruction, when enabled again, will write a new value to the first position of the sequencer data file.

Sequencer instructions are common in automation scenarios where the PLC performs a sequence of operations with the output device. As you become more familiar with the PLC, your experience with this instruction will grow...
SQL - Sequencer Loadamming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts
This completes the information on SEQUENCER INSTRUCTIONS.....
1. The Sequencer Output (SQO) instruction is used to send a sequence of data files to a destination.
2. The Sequencer Compare (SQC) instruction is used to compare an input value with a sequence of data file elements. If a match is found, a bit will indicate this in the control word...
3. The Sequencer Load (SQL) instruction is used to load word data into a sequencer data file.

The program shown below is the ladder logic program you will enter to demonstrate the sequencer instructions that you learned in the first part of this lesson.
Before you enter the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help us understand if the program is operating properly when we test it.
On the 5050-1 PC card, there is one switch that will be used for this program: the slide switch labeled "power", which is connected to I:0/2.
The slide switch is used to set the PLC to perform one of two operations. This allows us to load the sequencer file data into a specific location at any time, or sequence the data to the output.ut.

When the slide switch is in the left (OFF) position, three fill file instructions are used to place six words of information into six data words in file #B10 starting with word 1. Fill file is used since the second and third FLL instructions write data to multiple locations...

You may have noticed that this example is the same as the one discussed in the first part of this lesson. Laser one is attached to the first output bit and should be on for 1 second. Then, laser two (attached to output bit three) is on for 2 seconds. Finally, all outputs are off for three seconds...

When the slide switch is in the right (ON) position, the second and third rungs will be used. The second rung is a timer and is activated when the slide switch is in the right position. This timer counts for 1 second and then sets the done bit...

The third rung waits for the timer's done bit to be set. When this occurs, the timer resets, and the sequencer sends the next piece of sequential data. Every second, a new sequence data item is sent...
The operation of these instructions is straightforward. The example from the first section of the lesson was used to build your confidence in using the sequence instructions.
